rows.summary: A 2020 systematic review found 13 studies of 5-HTP in depressed patients and pooled 7; depression scores improved, but results varied widely and the reviewers judged the studies relatively weak because few included placebo groups, so most of the pooled result is a within-group change. A Cochrane review of tryptophan and 5-HTP found only two trials of sufficient quality, with 64 patients in total (one of them tested 5-HTP), and considered the evidence of insufficient quality to be conclusive. Graded C because almost none of the evidence is placebo-controlled.

No trial of 5-HTP in people with diagnosed insomnia was found in a PubMed search on 25 November 2026. One single-blinded randomized trial assigned 30 older adults to take 100 mg of 5-HTP daily for 12 weeks or nothing; there was no placebo. The authors reported improvement in some sleep-quality components, seen mainly in those who were poor sleepers at the start. The participants were not selected for insomnia, so this is too little to judge.

Results are mixed. A 2018 meta-analysis of 3 randomized trials in 151 people found better symptom scores and response rates with aloe vera than with placebo, but a 2026 meta-analysis of 3 studies found no significant difference and said the quality of many studies was limited. Individual trials were mostly null: a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial that randomised 58 people found no evidence of benefit at 1 month, with only a trend in diarrhoea-predominant patients; a crossover trial that randomised 110 people, of whom 47 completed it, found no difference in quality of life; and a randomized, double-blind trial completed by 160 people with all IBS subtypes found aloe extract no better than an inulin control after 4 weeks.

Two reports of randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, each describing 70 people given alpha-lipoic acid 1200 mg a day or placebo for 8 weeks, found no difference from placebo. One measured inflammatory markers (CRP, interleukin-6) and a marker of joint erosion; the other measured oxidative stress markers. Neither abstract reports joint counts, pain or a disease activity score, and neither says whether participants stayed on disease-modifying drugs.

In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 60 people with active disease took an Andrographis paniculata extract three times a day for 14 weeks. Joint pain intensity, the main outcome, did not differ significantly from placebo. Reductions in tender and swollen joints and in disability scores were reported as within-group changes in the extract group. The authors said a larger and longer trial is needed. The abstract does not say whether participants stayed on disease-modifying drugs.

In a three-armed, double-blind trial, 120 people with IBS were randomized to enteric-coated anise oil capsules, placebo or an active control for 4 weeks. At the end, 75% of the anise oil group, 35% of the placebo group and 52.5% of the active-control group were free of IBS symptoms. A 2020 review of herbal medicines noted that the positive herbal trials other than those of peppermint oil, aloe vera and asafoetida have not been replicated. The abstract does not report results by IBS subtype.

No randomized trial of artichoke leaf extract in IBS was found in PubMed searches on 25 November 2026. Two uncontrolled analyses exist, both in people who were taking the extract for indigestion. In a post-marketing surveillance study, a sub-group with IBS symptoms reported less severe symptoms after 6 weeks. In a subset analysis of an open postal study, 208 adults identified afterwards as having IBS were compared before and after two months; the proportion meeting IBS criteria fell by 26.4%. Both are within-group changes with no placebo comparison, and the authors of the first said a controlled trial was justified.

One randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial tested ashwagandha root extract with piperine (500 mg with 5 mg) for 90 days in 70 people with mild to moderate depression and anxiety; depression and anxiety improved in both groups and improved significantly more with the extract. The abstract does not say how depression was diagnosed, and no trial of ashwagandha alone in people diagnosed with major depressive disorder was found in a PubMed search on 25 November 2026. A 2026 meta-analysis of 22 trials in adults reported improved depression scores, but its abstract does not say the participants had diagnosed depression, and it called for high-quality trials to address heterogeneity. Graded C because the one trial found in depressed people is small and tested a combination.

A 2021 meta-analysis of 5 randomized trials in 400 adults found a small but significant effect of ashwagandha extract on overall sleep compared with placebo, more prominent in adults diagnosed with insomnia; results varied between trials. A 2024 meta-analysis of 5 randomized trials in 254 people with anxiety or insomnia found improvements in time to fall asleep, total sleep time and sleep-quality scores, but not in time awake during the night, and called for larger trials. In one randomized, double-blind trial, 60 people with insomnia took 300 mg of root extract or placebo twice daily for 10 weeks; time to fall asleep was significantly shorter with ashwagandha than with placebo at the end.

One small randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial was found. Sixty people with knee joint pain and discomfort (the abstract does not say that osteoarthritis was confirmed) took one of two doses of an ashwagandha root and leaf extract or placebo for 12 weeks; knee symptom and swelling scores fell compared with baseline and placebo at both doses. A 2025 network meta-analysis of botanical extracts for knee osteoarthritis reported that ashwagandha extract reduced stiffness scores compared with placebo. Graded C because the evidence rests on a single small trial.

A 2014 Cochrane review found moderate-quality evidence from four trials (651 people) that ASU 300 mg produced a small and clinically questionable improvement in symptoms after three to 12 months, with no difference from placebo in joint space width in two trials. A 2008 meta-analysis of four trials, all supported by the manufacturer, in 664 people with hip or knee osteoarthritis found less pain with ASU, with heterogeneous results and better chances of success in knee than in hip osteoarthritis. A 2019 meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials likewise found a benefit in knee but not in hip osteoarthritis.

Treatment: an 18-month trial in 409 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease tested high-dose folic acid, vitamin B6 and vitamin B12 against placebo and found no slowing of cognitive decline. A 26-week trial in 89 people with Alzheimer's taking a cholinesterase inhibitor found no difference in cognition or daily function. A 2024 meta-analysis of 5 trials in Alzheimer's found slightly better MMSE scores with B12 and folic acid but no difference on the ADAS-Cog or in daily life function. In mild cognitive impairment, a Cochrane review of 5 trials found no evidence of benefit on cognition; one 2-year trial found slower brain shrinkage on MRI. Prevention: a Cochrane review of 14 trials in 27,882 cognitively healthy adults found B vitamins probably have little or no effect on overall cognition. A Japanese cohort study linked higher dietary riboflavin (vitamin B2), measured from a single 24-hour food recall, to a lower risk of disabling dementia; this is an association from diet, not a supplement trial.

These have been tested almost entirely as add-ons to antidepressants: a 2018 meta-analysis in unipolar depression found no trials of folate or methylfolate alone against placebo. A 2022 meta-analysis found a small benefit when L-methylfolate was added to an antidepressant in adults with major depressive disorder (3 studies, 483 people). The 2018 meta-analysis found a significant benefit only for folate below 5 mg a day or methylfolate 15 mg a day added to an SSRI, and graded all the evidence low or very low quality. A 2016 meta-analysis of folic acid added to antidepressants found no significant difference from placebo. A 2015 meta-analysis found that short-term folate and vitamin B12 did not improve symptoms in adults with major depression treated with antidepressants, though longer use may lower the risk of relapse. A 2021 meta-analysis of 16 trials found no overall effect of vitamin B12 or B-complex on measures of depression; its participants were not selected for diagnosed depression.

In a double-blind trial in Germany, 323 people with Long COVID were randomized to 28 days of prednisolone, a combination of thiamine (vitamin B1, 100 mg), vitamin B6 and vitamin B12, both, or placebo. The B vitamins made no statistically significant or clinically meaningful difference to overall symptom severity.

In a 36-week double-blind randomized trial in 65 people with ME/CFS, yeast beta-glucan combined with vitamin D3, vitamin B6 and zinc was compared with placebo. Cognitive fatigue improved compared with the supplement group's own starting point; the abstract does not report a difference from placebo.

No randomized, observational or pilot studies of benfotiamine in people with Long COVID were found in a PubMed search on 23 November 2026. One registered single-arm study (NCT07745699) of a remote ketogenic diet and lifestyle programme for Long COVID included daily benfotiamine among several changes, so it cannot show the effect of benfotiamine alone, and no results from it are cited here. A different form of vitamin B1, thiamine, was tested with vitamins B6 and B12 in a randomized trial and made no difference (see B vitamins). Claims about benfotiamine in Long COVID rest on studies of other conditions or on laboratory reasoning.

One randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial studied berberine on its own, in diarrhoea-predominant IBS. In it, 132 people took 400 mg of berberine hydrochloride a day or placebo for 8 weeks; diarrhoea, abdominal pain and urgency became less frequent with berberine than with placebo. A 2026 meta-analysis of 19 trials in 1,489 people looked at berberine combined with brain-gut axis-targeted medicines for diarrhoea-predominant IBS, not berberine alone; it reported higher response rates with the combinations but judged the overall strength of evidence insufficient because of small samples and methodological weaknesses. No trials in constipation-predominant or mixed IBS were found in PubMed searches on 25 November 2026.

In a 36-week double-blind randomized trial in 65 people with ME/CFS, yeast beta-glucan combined with vitamin D3, vitamin B6 and zinc was compared with placebo. Cognitive fatigue improved compared with the supplement group's own starting point; the abstract does not report a difference from placebo.

In a 2-month randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 43 women with mild to moderate disease, one gram a day of black seed oil lowered CRP, the disease activity score (DAS-28) and the number of swollen joints compared with baseline and with placebo. A second randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 42 people, lasting 8 weeks, measured blood markers only, with mixed results. In another study, 40 women on disease-modifying drugs all took placebo capsules for a month and then black seed oil for a month; DAS-28 was lower after the oil. The abstracts of the two randomized trials do not say whether participants stayed on disease-modifying drugs. A 2020 systematic review concluded that the limited clinical studies did not show a change in inflammatory and oxidative markers. Graded C because the only randomized trial reporting clinical outcomes had 43 women; the other studies measured blood markers only or had no separate control group.

In a 60-day double-blind randomized placebo-controlled pilot study, 80 people with active disease who were maintained on the biologic drug etanercept added calcium fructoborate, sodium tetraborate (each supplying 6 mg of boron a day) or placebo; 72 completed it. Both forms of boron improved clinical scores and lowered ESR and CRP compared with baseline and with placebo. Graded C as a single pilot study.

A 2014 Cochrane review found high-quality evidence from two small trials (85 people) that 90 days of an enriched Boswellia serrata extract (100 mg) reduced pain by 17 points on a 100-point scale compared with placebo. A 2020 meta-analysis of 7 trials in 545 people found that boswellia may relieve pain compared with control groups. A 2024 meta-analysis of 13 knee trials found no significant overall effect, which the authors attributed to high heterogeneity, but a benefit over placebo in subgroup analysis. A 2018 meta-analysis found boswellia more effective than placebo but rated study quality low. A 2025 network meta-analysis of knee trials ranked boswellia as having the highest probability of being most effective for pain and stiffness among seven supplements and called for larger trials.

The one placebo-controlled trial found was a small pilot. In it, 47 people with moderate to severe knee osteoarthritis were randomized to 12 weeks of bromelain (800 mg a day) or placebo in addition to their usual treatment, and 31 completed the trial. There were no statistically significant differences between groups in the total WOMAC score, its subscales or quality of life, and the authors noted that the study's limitations support the need for a follow-up study. In a randomized, single-blind pilot study in 40 people with knee osteoarthritis that compared bromelain (500 mg a day) with diclofenac and had no placebo group, WOMAC scores did not differ between the groups after 4 weeks and the authors called the treatment difference inconclusive; the improvement reported at week 16 is a within-group change from baseline.

Two placebo-controlled trials tested a butterbur root extract. In a 4-month trial in 245 people, attacks fell by 48% at the higher dose tested (75 mg twice daily), against 26% with placebo; the lower dose was not better than placebo. A 12-week trial in 60 people also reported fewer attacks than placebo. A systematic review of both trials rated the evidence moderate and called for more studies of long-term safety.

One randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial tested single doses of 30 mg and 300 mg of cannabinol for one night each in 20 adults with physician-diagnosed insomnia disorder. Cannabinol did not significantly change the main outcome, minutes awake during the night measured in the sleep laboratory. The 300 mg dose shortened time to fall asleep and improved self-rated sleep quality, which were secondary outcomes. A single-night trial in 20 people is too little to judge.

A Cochrane review found two small trials of nabilone, a synthetic cannabinoid, with 72 participants in total, rated the evidence very low quality and found no convincing evidence of benefit. A 2026 meta-analysis pooling 2 randomized and 10 observational studies reported lower pain with cannabinoids, but rated the evidence low quality. An 8-week trial of a THC-rich cannabis oil in 17 women reported better Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire scores than placebo.

One randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial tested an oil containing 10 mg/ml THC and 15 mg/ml CBD for 2 weeks; 29 people with self-reported clinical insomnia completed it. After the cannabis oil period, 60% no longer met the questionnaire threshold for clinical insomnia, and light sleep measured by a wrist tracker increased by 21 minutes a night compared with placebo. The authors noted that effects were more pronounced in the second phase because of a period effect and loss of blinding. Graded C because this is a single small trial in which blinding was lost.

rows.product: Curcumin (in a topical mix with piperine and capsaicin)
rows.summary: In a 3-month randomized trial in 60 people, a scalp preparation combining piperine, capsaicin and curcumin was compared with 5% minoxidil, with no placebo group. Both groups had regrowth (effective in 63% with the mix and 70% with minoxidil), and the mix was not shown to be better than minoxidil. Because three ingredients were combined and there was no placebo, the trial cannot show what curcumin itself does, and it is not evidence that curcumin blocks JAK enzymes in people. No trials of oral curcumin or turmeric in alopecia areata were found.

A 2018 meta-analysis of 12 randomized trials in 791 participants (11 tested acetyl-L-carnitine on its own) found that it reduced depressive symptoms compared with placebo or no intervention across nine trials, with results that varied widely between trials, and found similar effectiveness to antidepressants in three trials. The effect appeared strongest in older adults, and the authors said large trials are needed to confirm or refute the findings. The abstract does not say how depression was diagnosed in the included trials.

A multicentre trial randomized 102 people to acetyl-L-carnitine or placebo. Both groups improved for the first 6 weeks; by week 10 the acetyl-L-carnitine group had better tender-point, depression and musculoskeletal pain scores. A smaller trial compared it with duloxetine, with no placebo group, and found improvements with both.

Neither trial used a placebo. An open-label 24-week trial randomized 90 people to acetyl-L-carnitine, propionyl-L-carnitine or both; mental fatigue improved with acetyl-L-carnitine and general fatigue with propionyl-L-carnitine, and 37% to 52% across the groups reported worse fatigue 2 weeks after stopping. A crossover trial in 30 people compared L-carnitine with the drug amantadine and reported improvement in 12 of 18 measures with L-carnitine.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of eight randomized trials in 619 people with osteoarthritis found better WOMAC function, total WOMAC and pain scores with L-carnitine than in control groups; the authors rated the quality of the included studies as mediocre and found heterogeneity between them. In a 12-week double-blind randomized trial in 76 obese women with knee osteoarthritis who were all on a low-calorie diet, L-carnitine (1000 mg) did not differ from placebo in pain, stiffness, physical function or total scores.

In a 24-week randomized trial in 200 people with fibromyalgia, 50 mg of plant-derived CBD a day was compared with placebo. Pain fell less with CBD than with placebo, by 0.7 points on a 0 to 10 scale, and the authors concluded the results do not support CBD as a pain-relieving supplement in fibromyalgia.

In a randomized, placebo-controlled pilot trial in 30 people with primary insomnia, 150 mg of CBD nightly for 2 weeks did not differ from placebo in insomnia severity, self-reported time to fall asleep, sleep efficiency or time awake during the night; objectively measured sleep efficiency was better with CBD after 2 weeks. In a double-blind, randomized crossover trial in 125 people with insomnia, 300 mg of CBD with added terpenes marginally increased the share of the night spent in deep and REM sleep, measured by a wrist-worn tracker, and had no effect on total sleep time. A 2023 systematic review found that only 2 of 34 studies of CBD and sleep focused on people with insomnia, and one of those was a case report. Graded C because the placebo-controlled trials in insomnia are small or showed little effect on insomnia symptoms.

One randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial tested an oil containing 10 mg/ml THC and 15 mg/ml CBD for 2 weeks; 29 people with self-reported clinical insomnia completed it. After the cannabis oil period, 60% no longer met the questionnaire threshold for clinical insomnia, and light sleep measured by a wrist tracker increased by 21 minutes a night compared with placebo. The authors noted that effects were more pronounced in the second phase because of a period effect and loss of blinding. Graded C because this is a single small trial in which blinding was lost.

In one randomized trial, 80 adults aged 18 to 35 with insomnia either inhaled chamomile oil for 10 minutes a day for 15 days or carried on with their normal routine. Sleep-quality and insomnia severity scores were better in the chamomile group afterwards. There was no placebo or other active comparison, and the authors said the result needs repeating against an active control. Graded C because the trial was not placebo-controlled.

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial in 34 adults with chronic primary insomnia tested 270 mg of chamomile extract or placebo twice daily for 28 days. There were no significant differences between groups in any sleep diary measure. A 2019 meta-analysis reported that only one randomized trial had tested chamomile for insomnia and that it found no significant change in insomnia severity. Meta-analyses that pooled trials in healthy adults and people with other conditions report better sleep-quality scores with chamomile, but that is not evidence in insomnia. Graded Negative because the only randomized trial in insomnia found no significant differences from placebo; this rests on a single small pilot trial.

A 2015 Cochrane review of 43 randomized trials, most in knee osteoarthritis and most of low quality, found that chondroitin was better than placebo for pain in short-term studies. The benefit became uncertain when the analysis was limited to trials with a large sample, appropriate allocation concealment or no pharmaceutical funding. A 2007 meta-analysis of 20 trials (3,846 people, knee or hip) found that small and less rigorous trials showed larger effects; in the 3 large trials analyzed by intention to treat, the effect was close to zero. In a 24-week five-arm trial of 1,583 people with knee osteoarthritis, chondroitin sulfate (1200 mg daily) was not significantly better than placebo. In a 6-month randomized trial in 162 people with hand osteoarthritis, chondroitin sulfate (800 mg daily) reduced hand pain and improved hand function more than placebo.

In a 24-week randomized trial of 1,583 people with knee osteoarthritis that compared glucosamine, chondroitin, both together, celecoxib and placebo, the combination was not significantly better than placebo overall; an exploratory analysis found a higher response rate in the subgroup with moderate-to-severe pain. A 2010 network meta-analysis of large knee and hip trials found a pain difference of 0.5 cm on a 10 cm scale for the combination and concluded that it does not reduce joint pain. A 2023 meta-analysis of 8 randomized trials in 3,793 people with knee osteoarthritis found a better total WOMAC score with the combination than with placebo but no significant difference in pain on a visual analog scale. A 2024 meta-analysis that pooled 3 trials of the combination found no reduction in pain and no improvement in function.

The randomized trials found in this search tested chromium picolinate in atypical depression. In a double-blind placebo-controlled pilot study in 15 people with major depressive disorder, atypical type, 7 of 10 people given chromium picolinate and none given placebo met responder criteria. A double-blind multicentre replication study then randomized 113 adult outpatients with atypical depression and found no significant difference between chromium and placebo on the primary efficacy measures; a supplemental analysis of 41 people with high carbohydrate craving favoured chromium. Graded Negative because the larger trial found no benefit on its primary measures.

In an 8-week randomized double-blind trial, 36 women took 4 capsules a day of 500 mg cinnamon powder or placebo. Compared with placebo, cinnamon lowered the disease activity score (DAS-28), pain scores, tender and swollen joint counts and CRP; ESR did not change. Graded C because the trial was small. The abstract does not say whether participants stayed on disease-modifying drugs.

rows.product: Collagen (undenatured type II collagen and collagen peptides)
rows.summary: A 2025 meta-analysis of 11 randomized trials in 870 people with knee osteoarthritis found better function and pain scores with oral collagen than with placebo, with results that varied a lot between trials. A 2019 meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials found lower total WOMAC and pain visual analog scores with collagen, but no significant difference in the WOMAC pain or functional limitation subscores. In a 180-day randomized, double-blind trial in 191 people with knee osteoarthritis, an undenatured type II collagen supplement lowered the overall WOMAC score more than placebo. A 2018 meta-analysis of supplements found that undenatured type II collagen was one of only two with clinically important effects on pain at medium term, and that no supplement had clinically important effects on pain at long term.

Results are mixed and mostly null. A 1993 randomized double-blind trial in 60 people with severe disease found fewer swollen and tender joints after 3 months of chicken type II collagen but not with placebo. A 24-week trial in 274 people testing four amounts found a significant difference from placebo only at the lowest amount and on only one of three sets of response criteria. Three other placebo-controlled trials found no significant benefit: one in 190 people who added bovine collagen to their existing medicines for 6 months, in which several clinical variables differed significantly and all of those favoured placebo, one in 60 people over 6 months, and one in 90 people with early disease over 12 weeks. In a 24-week double-blind trial in 503 people comparing chicken collagen with methotrexate, response rates were lower with collagen. Apart from the 190-person add-on trial, the abstracts do not say whether participants stayed on disease-modifying drugs.

rows.product: Probiotics with magnesium orotate and coenzyme Q10
rows.summary: One randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial tested this combination in 120 adults diagnosed with major depressive disorder for 8 weeks. Fewer people in the combination group still had a major depressive episode at the end of treatment, but depressive symptom measures differed from placebo only at 4 weeks, not at 8 or 16 weeks. Because the ingredients were given together, the trial cannot show what any one of them does. Graded B because this was a double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial in adults diagnosed with depression; it is a single trial with mixed outcomes.

Two recent meta-analyses pooled small randomized trials of CoQ10 and depressive symptoms, but most of the trials were not in people with major depressive disorder. In one, of 5 trials in 474 people, three enrolled people whose depression accompanied multiple sclerosis, breast cancer or polycystic ovary syndrome, and two enrolled people with primary depressive disorders (major depression and bipolar disorder). The other, of seven small trials across different clinical populations, found an effect on one rating scale but not on another and concluded that more data are needed. This is too little evidence in major depressive disorder itself to judge.

A 40-day randomized trial in 20 people found lower Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire and pain scores with CoQ10 than with placebo. A randomized crossover trial of a combined CoQ10, tryptophan and magnesium supplement, with two 3-month periods and 89 people completing it, found no benefit on its main outcome, fatigue; sleep quality and functional impact scores improved within the supplement group, and pain fell in both groups.

In a double-blind crossover trial, 121 people with Long COVID were randomized to take 500 mg of CoQ10 a day or placebo for 6 weeks each, and 119 completed both periods. CoQ10 did not reduce the number or severity of Long COVID symptoms compared with placebo; symptoms improved over time in both periods regardless of treatment. A 2024 living systematic review also found no compelling evidence for CoQ10.

Three placebo-controlled trials come from one research group; the first two share one trial registration. In an 8-week trial in 73 people, 200 mg of CoQ10 with 20 mg of NADH a day reduced fatigue impact scores more than placebo. An 8-week trial in 80 people found lower fatigue than with placebo; maximum heart rate on exercise testing fell from baseline within the supplement group, and pain and sleep did not change. A 12-week trial in 207 people reported improvements in cognitive fatigue and quality of life within the supplement group compared with its own starting point. A 2025 systematic review found the supplement studies in ME/CFS had a high risk of bias, and a 2020 review of 55 randomized ME/CFS trials listed CoQ10 plus NADH among 8 interventions with statistically significant results but found no treatment with consistent, reproducible benefit.

A 12-week double-blind randomized trial of ubiquinol-10 against placebo enrolled 43 people with chronic fatigue syndrome, and 31 completed it. The abstract states only that it improved several symptoms, without giving figures, so the size of any effect cannot be judged from the abstract.

A 2021 meta-analysis of 6 studies with 371 adults found shorter and less frequent migraine attacks with CoQ10 but no reduction in severity. A 2020 meta-analysis of 4 randomized trials with 221 people found about 1.9 fewer attacks a month, with no effect on severity or duration. A 2019 meta-analysis that pooled only 2 trials, with 97 adults, found no significant reduction in frequency.

In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 54 people with active disease took CoQ10 100 mg a day or placebo for 2 months; the disease activity score (DAS-28), pain score and tender and swollen joint counts were better in the CoQ10 group after the trial. A second double-blind randomized trial in 44 people, with the same amount and duration, measured blood markers only: an oxidative stress marker fell, and there was no difference in interleukin-6. The abstracts do not say whether participants stayed on disease-modifying drugs.

Creatine has been tested as an addition to other treatment. In an 8-week double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 52 women with major depressive disorder, creatine (5 g a day) added to escitalopram gave significantly greater improvement in depression scores than placebo added to escitalopram. A 2026 systematic review of 5 randomized trials (4 in major depressive disorder) also reported a benefit when creatine was added to cognitive behavioural therapy and no difference from placebo in a trial in female adolescents. A 2025 meta-analysis of 11 trials in 1,093 people with or without depression found a small average effect that was not clinically important, with very low quality evidence and signs of bias favouring creatine.

Two small randomized trials compared creatine with placebo. In a 6-month double-blind trial in 12 people with post-COVID fatigue, 4 g a day raised creatine levels in muscle and brain compared with placebo; fatigue fell compared with the start of the trial, which is not a comparison with placebo. In a 4-week single-blind pilot trial in 67 people, combined with physical activity, fatigue and grip strength improved more with 6 g a day than with placebo; the abstract does not report the same benefit for the 18 g a day group.

Creatine has been tested in small trials, two of them alongside exercise. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in postmenopausal women with knee osteoarthritis who all followed a lower limb resistance training program, physical function improved more with creatine than with placebo, while pain fell in both groups. In a four-week double-blind randomized trial in 40 people with knee osteoarthritis receiving physical therapy and resistance exercise, pain and overall knee scores favored the creatine group. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind trial in 18 people with mild to moderate knee osteoarthritis, creatine did not differ from placebo in knee symptom scores or muscle strength. Graded C because the trials are small and the positive ones tested creatine together with exercise.

rows.product: Curcumin (in a topical mix with piperine and capsaicin)
rows.summary: In a 3-month randomized trial in 60 people, a scalp preparation combining piperine, capsaicin and curcumin was compared with 5% minoxidil, with no placebo group. Both groups had regrowth (effective in 63% with the mix and 70% with minoxidil), and the mix was not shown to be better than minoxidil. Because three ingredients were combined and there was no placebo, the trial cannot show what curcumin itself does, and it is not evidence that curcumin blocks JAK enzymes in people. No trials of oral curcumin or turmeric in alopecia areata were found.

Treatment: in a 24-week placebo-controlled trial, 36 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease took 2 or 4 grams of curcumin a day or placebo; there were no differences in clinical or biomarker measures, and blood levels of curcumin were low. A 2019 meta-analysis found that, in the Alzheimer's trials it pooled, people taking curcumin tended to do worse than those on placebo on the MMSE. The trials are small, so this Negative grade rests on limited evidence. Prevention: trials in healthy older adults measure test scores, not dementia, and are not summarised here; claims that curcumin protects against Alzheimer's rest mainly on laboratory and animal work.

A 2020 meta-analysis (10 studies, 531 participants; in 7 of the 9 articles participants had major depressive disorder) found an overall significant effect of curcumin on depressive symptoms and suggested it might help when added to standard care, while warning that the small sample means the results should be interpreted cautiously. A 2021 meta-analysis of 10 trials in 594 patients found a smaller effect, judged three trials at high risk of bias and four unclear, and rated the evidence quality low, indicating great uncertainty.

No randomized, observational or pilot studies of turmeric or curcumin in people with fibromyalgia were found in a PubMed search on 23 November 2026. Claims about it in fibromyalgia rest on studies of other conditions or laboratory work.

In a placebo-controlled trial, 121 people with mild-to-moderate IBS were randomly assigned to capsules combining curcumin and fennel essential oil or to placebo for 30 days. Symptom severity scores fell more with the combination, and 25.9% of that group were symptom-free at the end compared with 6.8% on placebo. In a later open pilot study without a control group, 211 people (14% diarrhoea-predominant, 24% constipation-predominant, 62% mixed) reported lower symptom severity after two months; this is a within-group change. A 2020 review of herbal medicines noted that this positive trial has not been replicated.

No placebo-controlled trial of turmeric (Curcuma longa) or curcumin on its own in IBS was found in PubMed searches on 25 November 2026. A 2018 meta-analysis of three studies in 326 people found a beneficial but not statistically significant effect on IBS symptoms and called the evidence limited and heterogeneous. In a partially blinded pilot study, 207 volunteers were randomized to one or two tablets of turmeric extract a day for 8 weeks with no placebo group; about two thirds reported improvement, a within-group change, with no difference between doses. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of a different Curcuma species, Curcuma xanthorrhiza, found no benefit over placebo after 18 weeks. A 30-day trial that randomized 67 people with IBS and small bowel dysbiosis to a low-FODMAP diet with or without a curcumin and boswellia extract reported less bloating and abdominal pain with the supplement; there was no placebo. A 2024 systematic review of turmeric in digestive disorders judged most studies to be at high risk of bias.

A 2026 Cochrane review included 9 randomized trials in 1,245 people, all with knee osteoarthritis and none longer than three months. In the four placebo-controlled trials, turmeric may result in little to no difference in pain, function or quality of life (low-certainty evidence): pain was 0.72 points lower on a 0 to 10 scale, short of the 1.5 points taken as clinically significant. Turmeric may improve participant-reported treatment success, based on low-certainty evidence from 2 trials in 170 people. Earlier meta-analyses were more positive: a 2021 meta-analysis of 15 trials in 1,621 people found lower pain and better function than with placebo and effects similar to anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs), and a 2018 meta-analysis found benefit over placebo but rated study quality low, with most trials enrolling fewer than 100 people. No trials in hand or hip osteoarthritis were included in the Cochrane review.

A 2025 meta-analysis of 6 placebo-controlled randomized trials with 244 people found better disease activity scores (DAS28), joint counts, pain scores and inflammatory markers with curcumin, but rated the certainty of nearly every outcome very low and called for larger trials. A second 2025 meta-analysis of 7 randomized trials also found lower DAS28, ESR and CRP, with substantial differences between trials. In a randomized pilot trial, 45 people received curcumin 500 mg alone, the anti-inflammatory drug diclofenac alone, or both; DAS scores changed significantly in all three groups. A 2020 systematic review concluded that no conclusion could be drawn because the curcumin studies were of low quality. The meta-analysis abstracts do not say whether participants stayed on disease-modifying drugs.

The only study is an uncontrolled, open-label pilot in 41 people with fibromyalgia and/or chronic fatigue syndrome, with no placebo group. Participants reported better energy, sleep, mental clarity, pain and well-being after taking D-ribose. No randomized trials of D-ribose in ME/CFS were found in a PubMed search on 23 November 2026.

In a 14-day double-blind pilot randomized trial in adults with Long COVID, 25 of 31 participants completed beetroot juice or a placebo drink. Fatigue resistance and walking distance improved from baseline in both groups, with no difference between them; gut bacteria and some inflammatory markers changed with beetroot juice. This is a single small pilot trial.

rows.product: Essential oil blend (thyme, rosemary, lavender, cedarwood)
rows.summary: In a 7-month double-blind randomized trial in 86 people with alopecia areata, one group massaged a blend of thyme, rosemary, lavender and cedarwood oils in carrier oils into the scalp each day, and the other used carrier oils alone. Improvement was seen in 19 of 43 people (44%) with the essential oils and 6 of 41 (15%) with carrier oil. Because a four-oil blend was tested, the result cannot be attributed to rosemary or any single oil. Trials of rosemary oil in pattern hair loss (androgenetic alopecia) are a different condition and are not counted here. A systematic review of complementary therapies listed this blend among those with the best evidence for hair growth in alopecia areata.

In a placebo-controlled trial, 121 people with mild-to-moderate IBS were randomly assigned to capsules combining curcumin and fennel essential oil or to placebo for 30 days. Symptom severity scores fell more with the combination, and 25.9% of that group were symptom-free at the end compared with 6.8% on placebo. In a later open pilot study without a control group, 211 people (14% diarrhoea-predominant, 24% constipation-predominant, 62% mixed) reported lower symptom severity after two months; this is a within-group change. A 2020 review of herbal medicines noted that this positive trial has not been replicated.

A Cochrane review found 6 placebo-controlled trials with 561 people. The largest, in 218 people, found 0.6 fewer attacks a month with feverfew than with placebo; three small trials were positive, and two rigorous trials found no difference. The reviewers rated the evidence low quality. In one of those trials, of 147 people, feverfew did not reduce attacks overall, only in a small predefined subgroup.

rows.product: Gamma-linolenic acid (evening primrose, borage or blackcurrant seed oil)
rows.summary: A 2011 Cochrane review pooled 7 studies of oils containing gamma-linolenic acid and found lower pain intensity and less disability than with placebo; the reviewers called this moderate evidence of some benefit in relieving symptoms. In a separate randomized trial, 56 people with active disease took 2.8 g a day of gamma-linolenic acid or placebo for 6 months, and 14 of 22 on the acid had a meaningful response against 4 of 19 on placebo; the authors noted that it is usually taken in far lower amounts than the trial used. These abstracts do not say whether participants stayed on disease-modifying drugs.

rows.product: Garlic gel (topical, added to a steroid cream)
rows.route_note: applied to the skin, added to a steroid cream
rows.summary: In a 3-month double-blind randomized trial in 40 people with localized alopecia areata, everyone used a corticosteroid cream (betamethasone), and half also applied garlic gel while half applied a placebo gel. A good response was reported in 19 of 20 people in the garlic group, which the authors reported as significantly better than the control group; the abstract does not give the control group's response rate. Graded C because it is one small add-on trial.

Two reports of randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials each describe 70 women given garlic 1,000 mg a day or placebo for 8 weeks. In one, pain intensity, tender joint count, disease activity score (DAS-28) and fatigue fell more with garlic than with placebo, as did CRP, while ESR did not change. In the other, pain after activity and disability scores decreased compared with placebo. The abstracts do not say whether participants stayed on disease-modifying drugs.

One double-blind randomized controlled pilot trial was found in PubMed searches on 25 November 2026. Forty-five people with IBS took placebo, 1 g of ginger or 2 g of ginger a day for 28 days. Response rates were 57.1% with placebo, 46.7% with 1 g and 33.3% with 2 g, so ginger did not perform better than placebo. The trial was small, and its authors said larger trials are needed before firm conclusions can be drawn. The abstract does not report IBS subtype.

For prevention, a 3-month placebo-controlled trial in 107 people found no benefit of ginger extract. For acute attacks, a trial in 60 people in an emergency room found better pain response at 1 to 2 hours when ginger was added to an intravenous painkiller, and a trial in 100 people found ginger powder comparable to sumatriptan. A 2026 meta-analysis of 8 trials with 594 people rated the certainty of evidence low to very low and concluded it is too uncertain whether ginger is effective.

A 2015 meta-analysis of five randomized placebo-controlled trials in 593 people found a statistically significant reduction in pain and disability with oral ginger, described by the authors as modestly efficacious, and rated the evidence moderate quality. A 2020 meta-analysis in knee osteoarthritis found less pain with ginger capsules than with placebo but no significant difference in knee function, and concluded there was insufficient evidence to support oral ginger. A 2022 meta-analysis of three trials found that pain was the only clinical measure that fell significantly.

In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 70 people with active disease took ginger powder 1500 mg a day or placebo; the fall in disease activity score was significant within the ginger group and between the two groups. A second report, in 66 people given 1.5 g a day or placebo, found a decline in CRP. A 2020 systematic review said the risk of bias of the spice studies is difficult to assess and the data are too limited to recommend them in daily practice. The abstracts do not say whether participants stayed on disease-modifying drugs.

Treatment: a 2026 Cochrane review compared ginkgo with placebo. In 13 studies with 3,288 people with dementia, it found low-certainty evidence of small to moderate benefits at six months on global status, cognition and daily activities. In 12 studies of mild cognitive impairment, ginkgo probably had little or no effect. Prevention: two large placebo-controlled trials found no reduction in dementia. In one, 3,069 people aged 75 or older took 120 mg twice a day or placebo and were followed for a median of 6.1 years; the other followed 2,854 older adults for 5 years and found no reduction in progression to Alzheimer's disease.

A 2024 meta-analysis of 21 articles in 2,074 patients with depression found lower Hamilton depression scores with ginkgo than in control groups at 4, 6 and 8 weeks. Its outcomes included stroke and daily-living scales, which suggests that many of the trials were in depression after stroke rather than major depressive disorder; the abstract does not describe the trial designs, the control treatments or the risk of bias. No randomized trial of ginkgo in people diagnosed with major depressive disorder was found in a PubMed search on 25 November 2026. Graded C for those reasons.
No randomized or observational studies of ginkgo biloba in people with insomnia were found in PubMed searches on 25 November 2026.

Results are mixed and depend on trial size and funding. A 2017 meta-analysis of individual patient data from five industry-independent trials (1,625 people) found glucosamine no better than placebo for knee or hip pain or function at 3 months or 24 months. A 2010 network meta-analysis of 10 large trials in 3,803 people with knee or hip osteoarthritis found a pain difference of 0.4 cm on a 10 cm scale, smaller than the 0.9 cm set in advance as clinically important, with smaller effects in industry-independent trials. In a 24-week five-arm trial of 1,583 people with knee osteoarthritis, glucosamine (1500 mg daily) was not significantly better than placebo. A 2005 Cochrane review of 20 trials found a pooled improvement in pain, but not in the eight trials with adequate allocation concealment. A 2018 network meta-analysis of knee trials lasting at least 12 months found an association between glucosamine sulfate and less pain, with large uncertainty.

In a 24-week randomized trial of 1,583 people with knee osteoarthritis that compared glucosamine, chondroitin, both together, celecoxib and placebo, the combination was not significantly better than placebo overall; an exploratory analysis found a higher response rate in the subgroup with moderate-to-severe pain. A 2010 network meta-analysis of large knee and hip trials found a pain difference of 0.5 cm on a 10 cm scale for the combination and concluded that it does not reduce joint pain. A 2023 meta-analysis of 8 randomized trials in 3,793 people with knee osteoarthritis found a better total WOMAC score with the combination than with placebo but no significant difference in pain on a visual analog scale. A 2024 meta-analysis that pooled 3 trials of the combination found no reduction in pain and no improvement in function.

The main trial studied a narrow group: adults with diarrhoea-predominant IBS and increased intestinal permeability that began after a gut infection. In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 106 people completed 8 weeks of glutamine (5 g three times a day) or placebo; 79.6% of the glutamine group and 5.8% of the placebo group had a drop of at least 50 points in symptom severity score. The authors said large trials should now be done to validate the findings. A second randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 50 people with IBS on a low-FODMAP diet and added glutamine (15 g a day) or placebo for 6 weeks; 88% of the glutamine group and 60% of the control group improved by more than 45%.

No trial of glycine in people with diagnosed insomnia was found in PubMed searches on 25 November 2026. A 2012 review by the researchers who study glycine states that taking it before bedtime improved self-rated sleep quality in people with insomniac tendencies, but the original trial reports were not found in PubMed and could not be checked. A study by the same group gave 3 g of glycine or placebo before bedtime to healthy volunteers whose sleep was deliberately restricted and found less next-day fatigue; that is not a study of insomnia.

A 2021 systematic review included nine clinical trials of green-lipped mussel extract in osteoarthritis and pooled five of them: pain on a visual analogue scale was lower with the extract (effect size -0.46), which the authors called a moderate and clinically meaningful effect, while noting that the evidence is limited by the number and quality of studies. An earlier systematic review of four randomized trials set aside two because of possible un-blinding and inappropriate statistical analysis, and concluded from the two more rigorous trials that the extract may be superior to placebo in mild to moderate osteoarthritis. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind trial in 100 adults with knee osteoarthritis, green-lipped mussel powder (1,000 mg a day) improved pain and physical function more than placebo; the primary outcome, total WOMAC score, was significantly better only in the analysis limited to the 93 people who completed the study.

EGCG is also marketed as a natural JAK inhibitor. The only alopecia areata study found treated cell lines and blood immune cells from patients in the laboratory; it suggested EGCG lowered JAK2 expression in those cells. No studies of people taking or applying EGCG for alopecia areata were found.

In a 12-week double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 19 people who also received standard therapy, a drink containing 3 g of alpha-glucosyl hesperidin was taken every morning by 9 people and a placebo drink by 10. Three of 9 improved with hesperidin and 1 of 10 with placebo. Graded C because the trial was very small and the abstract reports no statistical comparison.

In a multicentre randomized placebo-controlled trial in 184 adults with mild insomnia, a valerian-hops combination taken for 28 days gave modest improvements in self-reported sleep, but few comparisons with placebo reached statistical significance and no sleep measure recorded in the sleep laboratory differed between groups. People taking the combination rated their insomnia as less severe than those on placebo after 14 days. A randomized, double-blind feasibility trial in 40 people with occasional sleep problems found about 22 minutes more sleep a night with a valerian-hops extract than with placebo in exploratory analyses.

A Cochrane review of 4 short double-blind trials in 141 people with depressive disorders, testing inositol alone or added to other treatment, found no clear evidence of a therapeutic benefit. A 2014 meta-analysis of 7 randomized trials in depression (including bipolar depression, major depressive disorder and premenstrual dysphoric disorder) found no statistically significant effect on depressive symptoms. In a controlled double-blind trial, adding inositol did not improve depression in people who had not responded to an SSRI antidepressant.

A 2023 meta-analysis included 9 randomized trials with 785 people with insomnia disorder and 120 with sleep disturbance. Compared with placebo, suanzaoren improved self-reported sleep quality in the short term; the placebo-controlled studies had a low risk of bias. Longer-term results were mixed, and the authors said the benefits and harms need testing in a larger trial because of small samples and variable study quality.

Results are mixed, and kava has reports of liver injury (see safety). In a multicentre randomized, double-blind trial, 61 people with sleep disturbances linked to anxiety took 200 mg of a kava extract or placebo daily for 4 weeks; sleep quality and feeling restored after sleep improved more with kava. A 2015 meta-analysis of herbal medicines for insomnia, which included kava, found no significant difference between any herb and placebo. A randomized trial that assigned 391 people with anxiety and insomnia to three groups (121 to kava, 135 to valerian and 135 to placebo) concluded that kava did not relieve anxiety or insomnia more than placebo. A pilot study in 24 people with stress-induced insomnia reported improvement in insomnia during 6 weeks of kava; its abstract describes no placebo group.

In a 28-day single-blind trial, 50 adults with Long COVID and persistent fatigue were randomized to L-arginine (1.66 g) with liposomal vitamin C (500 mg) twice a day, or placebo; 46 completed it. The supplement group walked further in 6 minutes, had better handgrip strength and blood-vessel function, and fewer reported fatigue. A secondary analysis found higher blood L-arginine levels. The trial was small, short and not double-blind, and a 2024 living systematic review found no compelling evidence for this combination.

The studies found in this search tested L-theanine as an addition to other treatment. In a six-week randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial, 60 people with major depressive disorder received sertraline plus either L-theanine (200 mg a day) or placebo; depression scores fell more with L-theanine, and response and remission rates at week 6 were higher. The authors named the small sample and short study period as limitations. In an 8-week open-label study, 20 people with major depressive disorder had lower depression scores after L-theanine was added to their current medication (a within-group change with no placebo group). Graded C because the one placebo-controlled trial found is small and short.

No meta-analysis or trial limited to people with diagnosed insomnia was found in a PubMed search on 25 November 2026. A 2025 meta-analysis of 18 randomized trials pooled people of all ages and health status and found small improvements in self-reported time to fall asleep, daytime functioning and overall sleep quality; the authors noted a lack of studies of L-theanine on its own. A 2026 systematic review of 13 trials of L-theanine alone reported benefits on sleep measures in adults and said trials in people with clinical insomnia are still needed. This evidence is about sleep quality in general, so it is too little to judge an effect on insomnia.

One randomized, double-blind, placebo- and reference-controlled trial tested a lavender oil preparation taken by mouth (80 mg a day) on its own for 8 weeks in 498 people with a mild or moderate episode of major depressive disorder. Depression scores fell 2.17 points more with lavender oil than with placebo on the Montgomery Asberg scale, and 2.59 points more with the reference antidepressant sertraline than with placebo. A second 2026 paper analyses individual symptoms in the same trial. The finding rests on a single trial.

A 2026 meta-analysis pooled 15 randomized trials of inhaled lavender oil in adults with primary sleep disorders or sleep disturbance linked to another condition. Sleep-quality scores improved more with lavender than with control, but results varied widely between trials, a statistical test suggested possible publication bias, and the authors said the findings should be interpreted cautiously. A 2025 review of 10 clinical trials in adults over 60 with sleep disorders, all using inhaled lavender, found improvement in 9 of them.

No trial of oral lavender oil in people with diagnosed insomnia was found in a PubMed search on 25 November 2026. One randomized, double-blind trial tested 80 mg of an oral lavender oil preparation once daily for 10 weeks in 170 outpatients with anxiety-related restlessness and disturbed sleep. Anxiety scores fell more than with placebo. A sleep-quality questionnaire was among the outcomes, and the abstract says the effect was more pronounced than with placebo on all outcome measures, but it gives no separate sleep result. This is too little to judge an effect on insomnia.

One double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study of a lemon balm extract reported lower insomnia severity scores with the extract than with placebo (6.8 against 9.7 points); its abstract does not give the number of participants or say whether they had diagnosed insomnia. A separate placebo-controlled trial in 100 women aged 50 to 60 with sleep complaints during menopause found better sleep-quality scores with a combination of valerian and lemon balm, which cannot show the effect of lemon balm alone. Graded C because the evidence for lemon balm alone is a single study with limited reporting.

rows.product: Palmitoylethanolamide with luteolin (for loss of smell)
rows.summary: For loss of smell lasting more than 6 months after COVID-19, a multicentre double-blind randomized trial in 185 people compared this supplement plus smell training with placebo plus smell training for 90 days. Smell test scores improved more with the supplement: 92% of the supplement group improved against 42% of the placebo group. It was tested only for smell loss, not for other Long COVID symptoms.

rows.product: Probiotics with magnesium orotate and coenzyme Q10
rows.summary: One randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial tested this combination in 120 adults diagnosed with major depressive disorder for 8 weeks. Fewer people in the combination group still had a major depressive episode at the end of treatment, but depressive symptom measures differed from placebo only at 4 weeks, not at 8 or 16 weeks. Because the ingredients were given together, the trial cannot show what any one of them does. Graded B because this was a double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial in adults diagnosed with depression; it is a single trial with mixed outcomes.

A 2023 meta-analysis of 7 placebo-controlled trials in 325 adults with depressive disorder found a significant fall in depression scores with magnesium and called for high-quality trials with larger samples. Individual trials disagree. In a double-blind trial of 37 people with recurrent depressive disorder, magnesium added to fluoxetine made no significant difference to depression scores compared with placebo added to fluoxetine. In a double-blind trial in depressed patients with magnesium deficiency, scores fell more with magnesium oxide than with placebo. An open-label randomized cross-over trial in 126 adults with mild-to-moderate symptoms found improvement after 6 weeks of magnesium chloride (248 mg of elemental magnesium a day), but it was compared with no treatment rather than placebo.

A review of the evidence on magnesium with malic acid found one randomized trial and concluded the combination makes little or no difference to pain or depressive symptoms. A separate 1-month randomized trial of magnesium against placebo found no difference in its main outcome, stress, although pain scores fell more with magnesium as a secondary outcome.

A 2021 meta-analysis found 3 randomized trials comparing oral magnesium with placebo in 151 older adults with insomnia. People taking magnesium fell asleep about 17 minutes sooner; total sleep time did not differ significantly. All three trials were at moderate-to-high risk of bias and the evidence was rated low to very low quality. A double-blind randomized trial in 46 older adults tested 500 mg of magnesium or placebo daily for 8 weeks and found lower insomnia severity scores with magnesium. A randomized trial in 155 adults who reported poor sleep (not diagnosed insomnia) tested 250 mg of elemental magnesium daily as magnesium bisglycinate and found a slightly greater drop in insomnia severity scores than with placebo at 4 weeks, with a small effect size. A 2026 systematic review of 12 randomized trials found inconsistent results and concluded that current evidence does not support oral magnesium as a routine treatment for insomnia, with low or very low certainty.

The only placebo-controlled trial, from 1991, gave magnesium sulphate by intramuscular injection, not by mouth. In 32 people over 6 weeks, 12 of 15 on magnesium and 3 of 17 on placebo said they felt better. No randomized trials of oral magnesium supplements in ME/CFS were found in a PubMed search on 23 November 2026.

rows.route_note: oral for prevention; intravenous for acute attacks
rows.summary: A 2016 meta-analysis of 21 randomized trials found that oral magnesium was linked to fewer and less intense migraine attacks and that intravenous magnesium relieved acute attacks, though some included trials did not use adequate randomization. A 2019 meta-analysis of 3 trials in 226 adults found no significant drop in migraine severity with oral magnesium (low strength of evidence). A 2014 meta-analysis of 5 randomized trials found no benefit of intravenous magnesium for acute pain relief.

A 2022 meta-analysis of 19 studies in 1,178 patients, covering both primary and secondary depression symptoms, found that melatonin was not significantly beneficial for depressive symptoms overall. A 2014 systematic review of 10 studies in 486 patients, only two of them in patients with depression, found no significant effect in its two meta-analyses. In a small double-blind trial in major depressive disorder, 10 people given slow-release melatonin with fluoxetine slept better than 9 given placebo with fluoxetine, but melatonin had no effect on the rate of improvement in depression.

One 8-week trial, described as double-blind and placebo-controlled although no placebo arm is listed, compared melatonin alone, the antidepressant fluoxetine alone, and the two combined. Fibromyalgia impact scores fell from baseline in the combination groups, and the authors concluded melatonin alone was also effective. A systematic review of 4 studies with 98 people found benefits in all of them but large differences between the studies.

Results are mixed. A 2013 meta-analysis of 19 placebo-controlled trials in 1683 adults and children with primary sleep disorders found that melatonin shortened the time to fall asleep by about 7 minutes and lengthened total sleep by about 8 minutes; the authors called the effects modest. A 2023 meta-analysis of 22 studies of melatonin or the prescription medicine ramelteon in insomnia disorder, in which 925 people received melatonin, found that prolonged-release melatonin shortened self-reported time to fall asleep by about 6 minutes compared with placebo. A 2022 meta-analysis of 24 randomized trials in chronic insomnia found no significant effect in adults on time to fall asleep, total sleep time or sleep efficiency. A 2017 American sleep medicine guideline suggested that clinicians not use melatonin for chronic insomnia in adults (a weak recommendation).

A 2026 systematic review found seven randomized trials in 391 people; pooling four of them, melatonin reduced moderate-to-severe IBS symptoms and pain frequency compared with placebo, with no significant difference in quality of life or sleep quality, and the authors called for larger, high-quality trials. An earlier meta-analysis pooled 4 trials with only 115 participants. In a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 40 people with IBS and sleep disturbances, 3 mg at bedtime for two weeks lowered abdominal pain scores more than placebo, with no difference in bloating or stool frequency. A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 136 people tested 6 mg a day for 8 weeks; its abstract reports improved IBS scores in people with and without sleep disorders and better quality of life than with placebo. The abstracts do not report results by IBS subtype.

In a 16-week double-blind randomized trial in 50 people with ME/CFS, melatonin (1 mg) with zinc (10 mg) once daily was compared with placebo. Physical fatigue was lower than with placebo at the final treatment visit, and the physical health summary score improved at every visit in the supplement group.

A 2026 meta-analysis of 9 randomized trials in 788 people found fewer headache days, shorter and less severe attacks, and more responders with melatonin than with placebo; the antidepressant amitriptyline was generally more effective for attack duration and severity. In one trial, 196 people were randomized to melatonin 3 mg, amitriptyline or placebo for 12 weeks; migraine days fell by 2.7 with melatonin and 1.1 with placebo.

In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 64 people took melatonin 6 mg a day or placebo. The disease activity score (DAS-28) and ESR fell from baseline with melatonin (a within-group change), but neither differed from the placebo group. The authors concluded that melatonin had no beneficial effect on DAS-28 and should not replace routine rheumatoid arthritis drugs. The abstract does not say whether participants stayed on disease-modifying drugs.

The trials of MSM alone are small. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind pilot trial in 50 people with knee osteoarthritis pain, MSM (3 g twice a day) lowered WOMAC pain and physical function impairment more than placebo, with no notable change in stiffness. In another 12-week randomized, double-blind trial in 49 people with knee osteoarthritis (1.125 g three times daily), physical function and total WOMAC scores improved more with MSM, WOMAC pain did not differ significantly, and the authors called the improvements small and of undetermined clinical significance. A 2008 systematic review described the evidence as positive but not definitive, and a 2018 meta-analysis of supplements placed MSM among those with statistically significant pain improvements of unclear clinical importance. In a 12-week randomized trial in 106 people with hand osteoarthritis, a combination of boswellia, pine bark extract, MSM and curcumin did not reduce hand pain more than placebo. Graded B because two randomized, double-blind trials each found some benefit over placebo; both were small, one was a pilot, their results for pain differed and the clinical importance of the improvements is undetermined.

Prevention: in COSMOS-Mind, a 3-year trial in 2,262 older adults, a daily multivitamin-mineral led to slightly better global cognition scores than placebo, and a meta-analysis of three COSMOS substudies estimated the effect as equal to about 2 years less cognitive ageing. The same trial found no reduction in new cases of mild cognitive impairment or dementia, though it had low statistical power for this. In the Physicians' Health Study II, 5,947 male physicians aged 65 or older who took a daily multivitamin had no cognitive benefit. Treatment: no randomized trials of general multivitamins in people with Alzheimer's disease were found in a PubMed search on 23 November 2026; a trial of a B-vitamin-based supplement is described under B vitamins.

In a 10-week randomized trial in 53 people with chronic fatigue syndrome, a supplement containing several vitamins, minerals and coenzymes was compared with placebo. There were no differences in fatigue, symptom count or daily functioning, and no patient reported full recovery. An older crossover trial in 15 people tested injections of a liver extract containing folic acid and vitamin B12 and found no difference from placebo.

N-acetylcysteine has been tested as an add-on treatment, and the meta-analyses mix people with major depressive disorder and bipolar depression. A 2020 meta-analysis of 7 double-blind placebo-controlled trials in bipolar depression and major depressive disorder found that it did not improve depressive symptoms compared with placebo. A 2024 meta-analysis of 12 studies in 904 patients found a small significant difference in favour of N-acetylcysteine, particularly in bipolar disorder, and said large trials were needed. In a 2016 meta-analysis of 5 studies that found a benefit, only 1 study enrolled people with major depressive disorder in a current episode.

Results are mixed. A 2024 meta-analysis of 4 randomized trials with 204 people concluded that NAC used as an add-on lowered disease activity and ESR, with no effect on oxidative stress. Two separate trials point the other way on disease activity: in a 3-month placebo-controlled trial in 74 people (600 mg twice a day), NAC did not improve the disease activity score, ESR or CRP compared with placebo; and in a 12-week trial in 51 people on standard treatment, the disease activity score and ESR did not differ between groups, though pain, global health and disability scores improved more with NAC. The authors of the 74-person trial stated that NAC should not be used as a replacement for routine rheumatoid arthritis medicines.

Three placebo-controlled trials come from one research group; the first two share one trial registration. In an 8-week trial in 73 people, 200 mg of CoQ10 with 20 mg of NADH a day reduced fatigue impact scores more than placebo. An 8-week trial in 80 people found lower fatigue than with placebo; maximum heart rate on exercise testing fell from baseline within the supplement group, and pain and sleep did not change. A 12-week trial in 207 people reported improvements in cognitive fatigue and quality of life within the supplement group compared with its own starting point. A 2025 systematic review found the supplement studies in ME/CFS had a high risk of bias, and a 2020 review of 55 randomized ME/CFS trials listed CoQ10 plus NADH among 8 interventions with statistically significant results but found no treatment with consistent, reproducible benefit.

Two placebo-controlled trials have mixed results. In a crossover trial in 26 people, 10 mg of NADH a day for 4 weeks was compared with placebo; 8 of 26 responded favorably to NADH against 2 of 26 to placebo. A larger 3-month trial, in which NADH or placebo was given for the first 2 months and 77 of 86 people completed it, found no difference in most outcomes and no difference in how patients or investigators rated its effect, although anxiety and maximum heart rate after exercise testing fell with NADH.

No randomized, observational or pilot studies of nattokinase in people with Long COVID were found in a PubMed search on 23 November 2026, and no Long COVID trial of nattokinase was found on ClinicalTrials.gov. Claims about it in Long COVID rest on laboratory work and on studies of other conditions.

rows.product: Nicotinamide riboside and other NAD+ precursors
rows.summary: In a 24-week double-blind trial, 58 people with Long COVID were randomized to nicotinamide riboside (2000 mg a day) or placebo first. It raised NAD+ levels within 5 weeks but did not improve cognition, fatigue, sleep or mood compared with placebo. Many people dropped out of the nicotinamide riboside group, and improvements seen within the group after 10 weeks were exploratory. A separate pilot study in 36 people gave NAD+ through skin patches together with low-dose naltrexone and reported improvements from baseline after 12 weeks; because both were given together, it cannot show the effect of NAD+ alone.

Treatment: a Cochrane review of 3 placebo-controlled trials in 632 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease found no convincing benefit of omega-3 supplements, and rated the evidence high quality. The largest, an 18-month trial of 2 g a day of algal DHA in 402 people, did not slow cognitive or functional decline. A 2024 meta-analysis of 14 studies, which also pooled a combined nutrient product, reported slower progression on the Clinical Dementia Rating scale but no difference on the MMSE, ADAS-cog or daily-activity scales. Prevention: a Cochrane review of trials in cognitively healthy older people found no benefit on cognition, and a 3-year trial in 1,680 older people with memory complaints found no effect on cognitive decline. In the Framingham cohort of 1,490 people without dementia, those with the highest red-blood-cell DHA had a 49% lower risk of Alzheimer's than those with the lowest; this is an association and does not show that DHA caused the difference.

A 2021 Cochrane review in adults with major depressive disorder pooled 33 placebo-controlled studies with 1,848 people and found a small to modest reduction in depressive symptoms that it judged unlikely to be clinically meaningful, with very low-certainty evidence and no difference in remission or response rates. A 2019 meta-analysis of 26 double-blind trials in 2,160 people found a benefit with formulations that were mostly EPA but not with those that were mostly DHA. A 2025 meta-analysis of 36 studies found a small overall effect, with significant heterogeneity and publication bias and no advantage over placebo in response or remission. Added to an antidepressant, a 2016 meta-analysis found a moderate to strong effect but signs of study bias. In children and adolescents, a 2024 Cochrane review of 5 trials in 228 participants found the evidence very uncertain.

One 12-week double-blind pilot trial in healthcare workers with Long COVID recruited 32 people, of whom 18 finished. Omega-3 did not significantly improve shortness of breath, cough, fatigue, or loss of taste or smell compared with placebo. The trial was designed to test feasibility and is too small to judge benefit.

Two 3-month placebo-controlled trials tested a capsule combining omega-6 (linoleic and gamma-linolenic acid) and omega-3 (EPA and DHA) fatty acids, with opposite results. A 1990 trial in 63 adults with postviral fatigue syndrome reported that 85% on the fatty acids and 17% on placebo felt improved at 3 months. A 1999 trial in 50 people, designed to repeat it using later diagnostic criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome, found no difference between the fatty acids and placebo. No trials of omega-3 on its own in ME/CFS were found in a PubMed search on 23 November 2026.

A 2023 meta-analysis of 9 randomized trials in 2,070 people with osteoarthritis found less pain and better joint function with omega-3 supplements than with placebo, while a 2022 meta-analysis of nutritional supplements reported that omega-3 caused no changes in osteoarthritis measures. For krill oil in knee osteoarthritis, a 24-week randomized trial in 262 people with significant knee pain and effusion-synovitis found that 2 g a day did not improve knee pain compared with placebo, whereas a 6-month trial in 235 adults with mild to moderate knee osteoarthritis found modest improvements in pain, stiffness and function with 4 g a day. A 2025 meta-analysis of 5 krill oil trials (730 people) found no significant improvement on a pain visual analog scale but better WOMAC pain, stiffness and function scores than with usual care. A two-year trial in 202 people compared high-dose with low-dose fish oil, without a placebo group, and found no additional benefit of the high dose.

A 2024 meta-analysis of 18 randomized trials with 1018 people found fewer tender joints with omega-3 supplements, while changes in the disease activity score (DAS28) and the inflammatory markers ESR and CRP were not statistically significant. Another 2024 meta-analysis, of 23 placebo-controlled trials, found only small effects on pain and on tender and swollen joint counts, with confidence intervals that included no effect; it rated the certainty mostly very low or low and concluded the clinical benefit might be limited. A 2012 meta-analysis of 10 trials found lower use of anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) at more than 2.7 g a day for more than 3 months, but joint counts did not improve significantly, and the 23-trial review suggested the painkiller finding may have been biased by inadequate blinding. These abstracts do not say whether participants stayed on disease-modifying drugs.

Two 3-month placebo-controlled trials tested a capsule combining omega-6 (linoleic and gamma-linolenic acid) and omega-3 (EPA and DHA) fatty acids, with opposite results. A 1990 trial in 63 adults with postviral fatigue syndrome reported that 85% on the fatty acids and 17% on placebo felt improved at 3 months. A 1999 trial in 50 people, designed to repeat it using later diagnostic criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome, found no difference between the fatty acids and placebo. No trials of omega-3 on its own in ME/CFS were found in a PubMed search on 23 November 2026.

In a small controlled study that did not report randomization, 23 people with patchy alopecia areata applied crude onion juice to the scalp twice a day and 15 applied tap water, for two months. Regrowth was seen in 20 of the onion-juice group (87%) at six weeks and in 2 of the tap-water group (13%) at eight weeks. The groups were unequal in size and were assessed at different time points.

In an open-label, non-randomized 6-week study, 43 people with Long COVID and 76 with ME/CFS took oxaloacetate; there was no concurrent placebo group, and results were compared with placebo results from an earlier, separate trial. Fatigue scores fell from baseline by up to 46.8% in the Long COVID group.

In an open-label, non-randomized 6-week study, 76 people with ME/CFS took one of three doses of oxaloacetate; there was no concurrent placebo group, and results were compared with placebo results from an earlier, separate trial. Fatigue scores fell from baseline by 22.5% to 27.9%.

Two randomized trials from one Chinese group had no placebo group. In 86 adults with mild to moderate alopecia areata, paeony glucoside capsules and compound glycyrrhizin tablets, another plant-derived product, gave similar response rates after 3 months. In 117 children with severe alopecia areata, adding paeony glucosides to glycyrrhizin tablets gave lower severity scores than glycyrrhizin alone, and better response rates at 6 and 12 months.

Total glucosides of paeony has been tested mainly as an addition to disease-modifying drugs. A 2018 meta-analysis of 8 randomized trials with 522 people found that adding it to methotrexate gave better overall response, lower ESR and fewer swollen joints than methotrexate alone, with no significant difference in CRP, morning stiffness or tender joint count; the authors rated the included trials as methodologically poor. A 2023 meta-analysis found it may improve the disease activity score (DAS28) and lower ESR and CRP, but called the trials low quality. A 2025 umbrella review rated the evidence for its effects on disease activity score and ESR as low quality.

rows.product: Palmitoylethanolamide with luteolin (for loss of smell)
rows.summary: For loss of smell lasting more than 6 months after COVID-19, a multicentre double-blind randomized trial in 185 people compared this supplement plus smell training with placebo plus smell training for 90 days. Smell test scores improved more with the supplement: 92% of the supplement group improved against 42% of the placebo group. It was tested only for smell loss, not for other Long COVID symptoms.

In a double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trial in 110 adults with insomnia disorder, 2 weeks of passionflower extract increased total sleep time measured in the sleep laboratory compared with placebo (P = 0.049). Sleep efficiency and time awake during the night improved in the passionflower group but did not differ from placebo. A second randomized, double-blind trial in 65 people with stress and insomnia found longer total sleep time with a passionflower extract than with placebo over 30 days. A trial of passionflower tea found better sleep-quality ratings than with placebo tea, but it studied 41 healthy adults, not people with insomnia.

A 2022 meta-analysis of 10 randomized trials in 1,030 people found peppermint oil more effective than placebo for overall IBS symptoms and abdominal pain, but rated the quality of evidence very low. An earlier meta-analysis of 9 trials of enteric-coated capsules in 726 people also found a benefit and judged the risk of bias low for most factors.
