Two later placebo-controlled trials were less favourable: a double-blind trial of 190 people found no significant difference in abdominal pain response or overall relief after 8 weeks, although the small-intestinal-release form did better than placebo on secondary measures of pain, discomfort and severity; and a 6-week double-blind trial at a single US centre found no significant differences between peppermint oil and placebo. A 2020 network meta-analysis ranked peppermint oil first for overall symptoms but warned of considerable uncertainty, with few trials at low risk of bias. The abstracts do not report results by IBS subtype.

The only study found in PubMed searches on 25 November 2026 was a registry study, not described as randomized or blinded, of 77 otherwise healthy people with IBS symptoms. Three groups took the extract (150 mg a day) or one of two other medicines used when needed, for 3 weeks. The number of painful attacks was comparable in all groups; pain on pressing the abdomen improved more in the extract group. There was no placebo group, and the abstract does not report IBS subtype.

A 2020 Cochrane review of pine bark extract found three osteoarthritis trials with 293 people and rated the evidence for knee osteoarthritis very low certainty, concluding that no definitive conclusions about efficacy or safety are possible. In one double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 100 people with knee osteoarthritis took 150 mg of pine bark extract a day or placebo for 3 months; the abstract reports within-group improvement in WOMAC and pain scores with the extract and no effect of placebo, without a direct comparison between the groups. In a 12-week randomized trial in 106 people with hand osteoarthritis, a combination of boswellia, pine bark extract, MSM and curcumin did not reduce hand pain more than placebo. Graded C because the only supportive result in a cited abstract is a within-group change and the Cochrane review rated the evidence very low certainty.

rows.product: Curcumin (in a topical mix with piperine and capsaicin)
rows.summary: In a 3-month randomized trial in 60 people, a scalp preparation combining piperine, capsaicin and curcumin was compared with 5% minoxidil, with no placebo group. Both groups had regrowth (effective in 63% with the mix and 70% with minoxidil), and the mix was not shown to be better than minoxidil. Because three ingredients were combined and there was no placebo, the trial cannot show what curcumin itself does, and it is not evidence that curcumin blocks JAK enzymes in people. No trials of oral curcumin or turmeric in alopecia areata were found.

One randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial tested ashwagandha root extract with piperine (500 mg with 5 mg) for 90 days in 70 people with mild to moderate depression and anxiety; depression and anxiety improved in both groups and improved significantly more with the extract. The abstract does not say how depression was diagnosed, and no trial of ashwagandha alone in people diagnosed with major depressive disorder was found in a PubMed search on 25 November 2026. A 2026 meta-analysis of 22 trials in adults reported improved depression scores, but its abstract does not say the participants had diagnosed depression, and it called for high-quality trials to address heterogeneity. Graded C because the one trial found in depressed people is small and tested a combination.

A 2019 meta-analysis of 11 randomized trials in 729 people with IBS or other functional bowel disorders found no difference between prebiotics and placebo in response (54% versus 63%, a comparison that rests on response data from 191 people: 52 of 97 versus 59 of 94), or in abdominal pain, bloating or quality of life, and none of the trials was at low risk of bias across all categories. Type mattered: inulin-type fructans made flatulence worse. A 2026 fibre meta-analysis found no significant overall effect on symptom scores except for galacto-oligosaccharides, which improved symptoms (2 of the included trials tested them). For synbiotics (a probiotic combined with a prebiotic), a 2024 network meta-analysis found no significant improvement, and two other meta-analyses said the data were too sparse to judge.

A 2025 meta-analysis of randomized trials in clinically diagnosed samples (23 trials, 1,401 patients; 18 trials tested probiotics for depression) found a significant reduction in depression symptoms with probiotics, with high heterogeneity between studies; prebiotics showed no significant effect. A second 2025 meta-analysis of 7 randomized trials in patients with depression also found fewer depressive symptoms with probiotics than with placebo. A 2025 network meta-analysis in adults with major depressive disorder, covering 42 placebo-controlled trials of antidepressants and of probiotics, prebiotics or synbiotics, rated the certainty of evidence moderate to very low and noted a lack of head-to-head trials between probiotics and antidepressants. Strains, doses and whether probiotics were used alone or with an antidepressant differ between trials.

rows.product: Probiotics with magnesium orotate and coenzyme Q10
rows.summary: One randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial tested this combination in 120 adults diagnosed with major depressive disorder for 8 weeks. Fewer people in the combination group still had a major depressive episode at the end of treatment, but depressive symptom measures differed from placebo only at 4 weeks, not at 8 or 16 weeks. Because the ingredients were given together, the trial cannot show what any one of them does. Graded B because this was a double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial in adults diagnosed with depression; it is a single trial with mixed outcomes.

A 2025 meta-analysis of 6 randomized trials in 424 people with insomnia found that probiotics lowered (improved) a standard sleep-quality score by about 2 points compared with control, rated moderate certainty. There was no significant effect on total sleep time or sleep efficiency, and the authors said the sample was limited. A 2026 meta-analysis of 39 placebo-controlled trials in 4094 adults and adolescents, not limited to people with insomnia, found a small improvement in sleep-quality scores (very low certainty) and no overall improvement in insomnia severity.

Results are strain-specific and the certainty is mostly low. A 2023 meta-analysis of 82 randomized trials in 10,332 people concluded that some combinations or strains may be beneficial, with moderate certainty for Escherichia strains on overall symptoms and low to very low certainty for almost everything else; only 24 trials were at low risk of bias across all domains. A 2026 strain-by-strain meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials found efficacy for Bifidobacterium longum 35624, Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, Lactiplantibacillus plantarum 299v, Saccharomyces cerevisiae CNCM I-3856 and Bacillus coagulans Unique IS2, but not for Escherichia coli Nissle 1917, Lactobacillus gasseri BNR17 or Lactobacillus casei Shirota. The 2023 review had reported moderate-certainty evidence of benefit for Escherichia strains, and its abstract does not name the strain. A 2026 meta-analysis of 40 studies found improved symptom severity scores but no significant change in quality of life, and rated certainty low because of inconsistency. A 2023 network meta-analysis found four strains and one mixture reduced bowel movement frequency in diarrhoea-predominant IBS.

A 2019 meta-analysis of 11 randomized trials in 729 people with IBS or other functional bowel disorders found no difference between prebiotics and placebo in response (54% versus 63%, a comparison that rests on response data from 191 people: 52 of 97 versus 59 of 94), or in abdominal pain, bloating or quality of life, and none of the trials was at low risk of bias across all categories. Type mattered: inulin-type fructans made flatulence worse. A 2026 fibre meta-analysis found no significant overall effect on symptom scores except for galacto-oligosaccharides, which improved symptoms (2 of the included trials tested them). For synbiotics (a probiotic combined with a prebiotic), a 2024 network meta-analysis found no significant improvement, and two other meta-analyses said the data were too sparse to judge.

In the largest trial, 463 people with Long COVID were randomized to a synbiotic preparation (a probiotic and prebiotic mix) or placebo for 6 months; more people in the synbiotic group had relief of fatigue, memory loss, difficulty concentrating, gut upset and general unwellness. Smaller placebo-controlled trials of other probiotic products, in 26 to 62 people, reported benefits on some outcomes, such as post-exercise malaise, breathing difficulty, or anxiety and depression scores, but not on others. A 14-day trial in 200 people reported less fatigue with a combined enzyme and probiotic supplement, so the effect of the probiotic alone cannot be separated. A 2024 living systematic review found no compelling evidence for combined probiotics and prebiotics. Each trial tested a different product.

Small placebo-controlled trials have mostly measured outcomes other than fatigue. In a 2-month pilot trial in 39 people, a Lactobacillus casei probiotic reduced anxiety scores. In a trial including 48 people with chronic fatigue syndrome, a Bifidobacterium infantis probiotic lowered blood markers of inflammation. In a 3-month trial in 26 people with ME/CFS after COVID-19, general fatigue fell in both the synbiotic and placebo groups, while post-exercise malaise improved more with the synbiotic. A 2018 systematic review judged the evidence for probiotics in ME/CFS poor and insufficient.

Results differ by strain and the trials are few. A 2024 meta-analysis of three randomized studies (501 people) found fewer symptoms with one Lactobacillus casei strain but no apparent effect with the other probiotics reviewed. A 2025 meta-analysis of five randomized trials in 694 people with knee osteoarthritis found lower total WOMAC and pain scores than in control groups, with no significant difference in stiffness, and said the results need validating in large studies. In a 12-week randomized, triple-blind trial in 70 overweight or obese people with knee osteoarthritis, Saccharomyces boulardii reduced pain more than placebo, and in a 12-week exploratory randomized, double-blind trial in 100 people with chronic knee pain, a Latilactobacillus sakei strain improved WOMAC and pain scores more than placebo.

Results are mixed. A 2022 meta-analysis covering 8 trials in 344 people with rheumatoid arthritis found lower CRP with probiotics, but no difference from placebo in the disease activity score (DAS28) once trials at high risk of bias were excluded; the authors said the evidence does not allow probiotics to be proposed for disease control. A 2017 meta-analysis of 9 trials in 361 people also found no difference in disease activity score. A 2023 meta-analysis of 12 trials of gut-microbe supplements used as add-on therapy found a lower disease activity score but no significant effect on pain or ESR. In one randomized double-blind trial in women on stable medication, 46 of whom were analysed, 8 weeks of Lactobacillus casei lowered CRP, tender and swollen joint counts and DAS28.

A 2026 meta-analysis of 30 randomized trials in 1,904 people with IBS found that, in the 16 trials (1,293 people) that reported clinical response, 52% responded to fibre supplements and 44% to control, with a benefit for psyllium specifically; pooled symptom scores did not differ significantly, and results could not be broken down by IBS subtype for most outcomes. A 2014 meta-analysis of 14 trials in 906 people found the benefit only in trials of soluble fibre, and a 2015 meta-analysis reached the same conclusion while noting a moderate risk of bias. In a 12-week primary-care trial of 275 people, more responded to 10 g of psyllium than to placebo in the first month (57% versus 35%) and the second month; quality of life did not differ.

In a 12-week double-blinded randomized trial, 86 people took a 500 mg purslane capsule twice a day or placebo, and 77 completed the study. The abstract reports that pain scores, tender and swollen joint counts and the disease activity score (DAS28) fell in the purslane group, without stating a comparison with placebo for these; only morning stiffness and the physician's global assessment are stated as lower than in the placebo group at the end of the trial. The abstract does not say whether participants stayed on disease-modifying drugs.

Quercetin is often listed as a natural JAK inhibitor, but the only alopecia areata study found was in mice: hair regrew in mice with alopecia areata given quercetin injections under the skin, and not in sham-treated mice. No human studies were found. Approved JAK inhibitor medicines are a different thing: baricitinib, the first JAK inhibitor approved for severe alopecia areata in the USA and EU, was tested in two placebo-controlled phase 3 trials in people. Laboratory findings for quercetin do not show it works like these medicines.

In an 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 50 women took quercetin 500 mg a day or placebo. Morning stiffness and pain fell with quercetin, and disease activity (DAS-28) and disability scores decreased compared with placebo. Tender and swollen joint counts did not differ between groups, and the change in ESR was not significant. Graded C because this is a single trial that was small and short. The abstract does not say whether participants stayed on disease-modifying drugs.

No randomized, observational, pilot or laboratory studies of resveratrol in alopecia areata were found in a PubMed search on 23 November 2026. Claims that it acts as a natural JAK inhibitor for hair loss rest on research in other conditions.

In a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial at three centers, 142 adults with painful knee osteoarthritis took oral resveratrol (40 mg twice a day for a week, then 20 mg twice a day) or placebo. At 3 months the reduction in knee pain was almost identical in the two groups; the authors noted that the trial was underpowered. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized trial in 110 people with knee osteoarthritis, resveratrol (500 mg a day) added to the anti-inflammatory drug meloxicam improved pain and function more than placebo added to meloxicam over 90 days. A 16-week randomized, placebo-controlled trial in 123 people aged 63 to 75 reported lower WOMAC scores and less pain during walking with resveratrol (500 mg a day); its abstract does not state how these changes compared with the placebo group.

In a randomized controlled trial without a placebo, 100 people were divided into two groups of 50: one took a resveratrol capsule of 1 g a day with their conventional treatment for 3 months, and the other had the regular treatment only. Swollen and tender joint counts, the 28-joint disease activity score, CRP and ESR were lower in the resveratrol group. Graded C because the comparison group received no placebo.

Three randomized trials give mixed results. In a 12-week placebo-controlled trial, 57 people with mild to moderate major depressive disorder received rhodiola extract, sertraline or placebo; there was no significant difference between the groups. In a 6-week double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 89 people with mild to moderate depression, depression scores improved significantly within the two rhodiola groups and not within the placebo group (a within-group change). In a 12-week double-blind trial in 100 people, depression scores fell more when rhodiola at 0.6 g a day was added to sertraline than with sertraline and placebo.

A 2022 meta-analysis of 8 randomized trials and 1 controlled trial, with 673 people, found fewer migraine days, shorter and less frequent attacks and lower pain scores with riboflavin, and concluded that 400 mg a day for three months had a significant effect. Results varied a lot between trials for migraine days and pain. A 2017 systematic review of 11 trials described consistent benefit in adults but mixed results in children and adolescents.

A 2008 meta-analysis pooled three randomized trials of rose hip powder in 287 people, all supported by the manufacturer, with a median duration of 3 months. Pain scores fell more with rose hip powder than with placebo, with consistent results across the trials; the authors called the data sparse and asked for independent replication in a large, long-term trial. In a randomized, double-blind crossover trial in 94 people with hip or knee osteoarthritis, 5 g of rose hip powder daily reduced WOMAC pain compared with placebo after 3 weeks.

In a 6-month randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 89 people, rose hip powder 5 g a day was compared with placebo. Disability scores (the trial's main outcome) improved slightly with rose hip and worsened slightly with placebo, a significant difference. Pain scores and use of pain medicines did not differ between groups, and the difference in disease activity score (DAS-28) did not reach statistical significance (p=0.056). The authors describe rose hip as an additional treatment.

A 2026 meta-analysis of 34 randomized trials in 1,769 adults found lower scores on a self-rated depression scale with saffron (14 trials, 817 people) but no significant effect on the clinician-rated Hamilton scale; it rated the certainty of evidence moderate, and its abstract does not say how many participants had diagnosed depression. A 2019 meta-analysis limited to people with mild to moderate depression pooled nine trials and found saffron more effective than placebo. A 2013 meta-analysis in adults with major depressive disorder included only 5 trials and called for larger trials by research teams outside Iran. Compared directly with SSRI antidepressants in 8 trials, saffron showed no significant difference in depressive symptoms; that comparison does not show that saffron can replace prescribed treatment.

A 2022 meta-analysis of 8 articles with 431 participants found better sleep quality with saffron than with placebo (very low-quality evidence) and longer sleep duration (moderate-quality evidence). The pooled difference in insomnia severity favoured saffron but was not statistically significant (p = 0.08). A second 2022 meta-analysis of randomized trials found lower (better) sleep-quality scores with saffron than with placebo; it pooled healthy adults with people who had insomnia, type 2 diabetes or were on methadone maintenance treatment, so it is not limited to insomnia.

In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 66 women with active disease took saffron 100 mg a day or placebo. Tender and swollen joint counts, pain scores and the disease activity score (DAS28) improved with saffron compared with placebo; differences in inflammatory and oxidative blood markers were not significant between groups. The trial abstract does not say whether participants stayed on disease-modifying drugs. A 2021 systematic review of saffron added to standard treatment in rheumatic diseases found the evidence not enough to establish a direction of effect.

A 2016 Cochrane review of 8 randomized trials in adults diagnosed with major depression, which accepted both oral and injected SAMe, found no strong evidence that SAMe on its own differed from placebo (2 studies, very low quality evidence). Added to an SSRI antidepressant, SAMe was superior to placebo in one study of 73 people (low quality evidence). A 2024 meta-analysis of 14 trials in 1,522 people found no significant difference between SAMe and placebo, either alone or as an add-on. In a 12-week double-blind analysis of 144 adults with major depressive disorder (a subsample from one site of a two-site study), SAMe at 1600 to 3200 mg a day improved depression scores more than placebo, while the comparison antidepressant did not separate from placebo. The same abstract notes that the full two-site study showed no significant difference between groups, because of site differences, and calls the single-site results preliminary.

Three small placebo-controlled trials were published between 1987 and 1997. A 6-week trial of oral SAMe in 44 people found less pain, fatigue and morning stiffness than with placebo, but no change in tender points. A crossover trial in 17 people found fewer tender points. A 10-day trial of intravenous SAMe in 34 people found no effect on its main outcome.

A 2009 Cochrane review of four placebo-controlled trials in 656 people with knee or hip osteoarthritis found a small difference in pain that was not statistically significant and no clear effect on function. The reviewers judged the trials to be of poor quality, called the review inconclusive and advised against routine use. A 2002 meta-analysis of 11 randomized trials found that SAMe improved functional limitation, but not pain, compared with placebo, based on only 2 studies, and that it appeared comparable with NSAIDs.

Results are mixed. A 2025 meta-analysis of 7 randomized trials with 367 people found lower pain scores and a lower joint tenderness index with selenium, but no significant effect on ESR, CRP, morning stiffness or joint swelling. Two separate trials found no difference from placebo: a double-blind trial in 55 people given selenium-enriched yeast for 90 days concluded there was no clinical benefit, and a 12-week double-blind trial in 59 people found no between-group difference in disease activity scores. The abstracts do not say whether participants stayed on disease-modifying drugs.

Senna is a stimulant laxative. No randomized or observational studies of senna in people with IBS, including constipation-predominant IBS, were found in PubMed searches on 25 November 2026. Evidence from chronic constipation without IBS does not count for this page.

In a 6-week randomized, triple-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 44 women took sesamin 200 mg a day or placebo. CRP and other inflammatory markers fell in the sesamin group compared with placebo, and the abstract reports fewer tender joints and less severe pain with sesamin, without stating whether that was a comparison with placebo. Graded C because the trial was small and short. The abstract does not say whether participants stayed on disease-modifying drugs.

Studied on its own, not added to an antidepressant. A 2008 Cochrane review of 29 randomized double-blind trials in 5,489 people with major depression found more responders with hypericum extracts than with placebo, but the placebo-controlled results varied markedly: the response rate ratio was 1.28 in nine larger trials and 1.87 in nine smaller ones, and trials from German-speaking countries were more favourable. A 2016 review of 35 randomized trials in 6,993 adults with major depressive disorder found St John's wort superior to placebo and not significantly different from antidepressant medication in mild and moderate depression (moderate quality of evidence), and noted that heterogeneity and a lack of research in severe depression reduce the quality of the evidence. A 2026 network meta-analysis of nutraceutical trials in major depressive disorder rated its confidence in the evidence low to very low.

In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 70 people with IBS (29% constipation-predominant, 37% diarrhoea-predominant, 31% mixed) took St John's wort or placebo for 12 weeks. Both groups improved, and the placebo group had significantly lower bowel symptom scores at 12 weeks. The authors concluded that St John's wort was less effective than placebo.

In a double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-centre trial, 208 people with IBS were randomly assigned to a preparation of nine plant extracts, a six-extract version, bitter candytuft extract alone, or placebo. At 4 weeks both combinations had reduced abdominal pain scores and IBS symptom scores significantly more than placebo; bitter candytuft alone did not differ from placebo. A 2020 review of herbal medicines noted that the positive herbal trials other than those of peppermint oil, aloe vera and asafoetida have not been replicated. The abstract does not report results by IBS subtype.

Two very small crossover pilot studies tested tart cherry juice in older adults with insomnia. In a randomized, double-blind crossover study in 15 people, 2 weeks of a tart cherry juice blend reduced minutes awake during the night compared with a placebo drink, with no difference in time to fall asleep, total sleep time or sleep efficiency; the authors noted the effects were considerably smaller than those of hypnotic medicines and cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia. In a placebo-controlled crossover study, the 8 people who finished slept 84 minutes longer in the sleep laboratory after 2 weeks of cherry juice (240 mL twice a day); most questionnaires showed no difference.

Extracts of thunder god vine have been tested both alone and with methotrexate. A 2023 meta-analysis of 14 randomized trials with 1446 people found higher response and remission rates when the extract was added to methotrexate than with methotrexate alone; the authors said higher-quality double-blind trials could change these conclusions. In an open-label randomized trial in 207 people, 55.1% reached a 50% improvement response with the extract alone, 46.4% with methotrexate alone and 76.8% with both; people in the single-drug groups whose disease activity score had fallen by less than 30% at week 12 were switched to the combination. In a randomized trial in 121 people who had stopped disease-modifying drugs, more people responded to the extract than to sulfasalazine, but outcome data were available for only 62 people at 24 weeks. A Cochrane review said these products may reduce some symptoms but that oral use may be associated with several side effects.

A Cochrane review of tryptophan and 5-HTP located 108 trials but judged only two, with 64 patients in total, to be of sufficient quality (one of them tested L-tryptophan); those two suggested the substances were better than placebo, and the reviewers considered the evidence of insufficient quality to be conclusive. In a double-blind trial in older hospital patients with mild to moderate depression, 6 grams of L-tryptophan a day was no different from placebo over six weeks. In a randomized double-blind trial of 30 people with major depressive disorder, tryptophan added to fluoxetine lowered depression scores more than placebo in the first week only. Graded C because the placebo-controlled trials are small and mostly old and their results conflict.

The trials in insomnia are small and old. In a double-blind crossover study in 39 people with chronic insomnia, 2 g of L-tryptophan was better than a very low comparison dose only in the group that took the full dose first. In a double-blind placebo-controlled study in which 49 of 57 people with chronic insomnia finished, a tryptophan-rich protein source with carbohydrate and pharmaceutical-grade tryptophan with carbohydrate improved insomnia measures, while carbohydrate alone did not. A 2022 meta-analysis pooling 4 articles found that tryptophan shortened time awake during the night but did not affect other sleep measures; its abstract does not say the participants had insomnia. A 2017 American sleep medicine guideline suggested that clinicians not use tryptophan for chronic insomnia (a weak recommendation). Graded C rather than B because the insomnia trials are small and their results are inconsistent.

Results are mixed and lean towards little measurable effect. A 2010 meta-analysis of 18 randomized placebo-controlled trials found that people taking valerian were more likely to say their sleep had improved (relative risk 1.37), but the time to fall asleep differed from placebo by less than a minute and sleep-quality scores did not differ. A 2006 meta-analysis of 16 trials in 1093 people found a similar yes-or-no benefit, with evidence of publication bias and methodological problems in most studies. A 2015 meta-analysis of herbal medicines in 1602 people with insomnia found no significant difference between any herb, including valerian, and placebo. In a randomized trial run over the internet, 391 people with anxiety and insomnia were assigned to three groups; the 135 given valerian and the 135 given placebo had similar improvements in sleep over 4 weeks. A 2024 randomized trial in 80 adults with sleep complaints found better sleep-quality scores with a valerian extract than with placebo over 8 weeks. A 2017 American sleep medicine guideline suggested that clinicians not use valerian for chronic insomnia (a weak recommendation).

In a multicentre randomized placebo-controlled trial in 184 adults with mild insomnia, a valerian-hops combination taken for 28 days gave modest improvements in self-reported sleep, but few comparisons with placebo reached statistical significance and no sleep measure recorded in the sleep laboratory differed between groups. People taking the combination rated their insomnia as less severe than those on placebo after 14 days. A randomized, double-blind feasibility trial in 40 people with occasional sleep problems found about 22 minutes more sleep a night with a valerian-hops extract than with placebo in exploratory analyses.

In a 28-day single-blind trial, 50 adults with Long COVID and persistent fatigue were randomized to L-arginine (1.66 g) with liposomal vitamin C (500 mg) twice a day, or placebo; 46 completed it. The supplement group walked further in 6 minutes, had better handgrip strength and blood-vessel function, and fewer reported fatigue. A secondary analysis found higher blood L-arginine levels. The trial was small, short and not double-blind, and a 2024 living systematic review found no compelling evidence for this combination.

In a multicenter, double-blind, randomized crossover trial, 133 people with hip or knee osteoarthritis took one gram of calcium ascorbate or placebo daily for about 14 days each. Pain was 4.6 mm lower on a 100 mm scale with calcium ascorbate than with placebo, an effect the authors described as less than half that commonly reported for NSAIDs. In a prospective cohort study, self-reported vitamin C supplement use was not associated with progression of existing knee osteoarthritis, although users without knee osteoarthritis at the start were less likely to develop it. A 2021 review called the data controversial and said more randomized placebo-controlled trials are needed. Graded B because the multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial found a statistically significant benefit; each treatment period lasted only about 14 days, so the trial does not show whether the effect lasts with longer use.

rows.product: Vitamin D (injected or applied to the scalp)
rows.route_note: injected into patches or applied to the scalp
rows.summary: All the treatment studies found used vitamin D3 injected into bald patches or calcipotriol, a vitamin D analogue applied to the scalp; no randomized trials of oral vitamin D supplements in alopecia areata were found in a PubMed search on 23 November 2026, and the authors of a planned 2022 systematic review said there is no conclusive evidence for supplementation. In a randomized trial in 60 adults with patchy alopecia areata, up to 3 injections of vitamin D3 gave more improvement than saline injections. In a 3-month randomized trial in 60 people, scalp severity scores improved from baseline with calcipotriol, ultraviolet B light, or both, but not with placebo. A 2026 meta-analysis found benefit for injected vitamin D3, an uncertain effect for topical vitamin D3 (the confidence interval crossed zero), and lower efficacy for injected vitamin D3 than for injected corticosteroid, based on a small number of trials. Separately, a meta-analysis of 14 observational studies found lower blood vitamin D levels in people with alopecia areata than in controls; that is an association, not evidence that supplements help.

Treatment: a 12-month trial in 210 people with Alzheimer's disease compared 800 IU of vitamin D a day with placebo and reported a larger increase in full-scale IQ and better scores on several cognitive subtests, with lower amyloid-related blood markers; the authors called for larger, longer trials. Prevention: in two substudies of the VITAL trial in older adults, 2,000 IU of vitamin D3 a day did not change the rate of cognitive decline over 2 to 3 years. A Cochrane review found no effect of 400 IU of vitamin D3 with calcium on dementia incidence. In a cohort of 12,388 people without dementia, taking vitamin D was associated with 40% lower dementia incidence; a cohort study cannot show that vitamin D caused this.

A 2019 meta-analysis of 4 randomized trials in 948 people with clinically diagnosed major depression (vitamin D was given by mouth in three and by injection in one) found a moderate improvement in depression ratings and called the finding tentative because of the small number of trials and methodological bias in some. A 2023 meta-analysis of 18 placebo-controlled trials in 1,980 depressed patients found vitamin D superior to placebo, with results that varied widely between trials and a benefit in adults but not in children and adolescents; some trials gave intermittent high doses by mouth or a single high dose by injection into muscle; concurrent antidepressant use did not change the effect. A 2024 meta-analysis of 18 trials in adults with primary depression found a small overall effect and none in people whose vitamin D level was below 50 nmol/L. A 2026 network meta-analysis described the pooled effect of vitamin D3 in its low risk-of-bias analysis as higher than expected or unrealistic and rated confidence in the evidence low to very low.

Two meta-analyses compared vitamin D with placebo or a control group. One, limited to randomized trials, pooled 5 studies with 315 people and found lower Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire scores but no difference in pain on a visual scale. The other, with 4 studies in each analysis, found lower pain scores and called for better trials.

No meta-analysis or trial of vitamin D limited to people with diagnosed insomnia was found in a PubMed search on 25 November 2026. Two 2022 meta-analyses of supplementation studies, not limited to people with insomnia, found better sleep-quality scores with vitamin D than with placebo or control. One of them concluded that results for sleep disorders were not unanimous and that the effect on sleep quantity and sleep disorders needs more study.

Results are mixed. Five meta-analyses published in 2022 and 2023 disagreed: three found better IBS symptom severity scores with vitamin D than with placebo, and two, including one of 6 trials in 616 people, found no significant effect on symptom severity but a better quality-of-life score. One of the reviews listed small samples, young participants and varied dosing as limitations. A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 135 people in the UK, 60% of whom had low vitamin D at the start, tested 3,000 IU a day for 12 weeks and found no difference in symptom severity or quality of life. The abstracts do not report results by IBS subtype.

In an 8-week double-blind randomized trial in 80 people with post-COVID fatigue or neuropsychiatric symptoms, weekly high-dose vitamin D (60,000 IU) was compared with placebo. Fatigue, anxiety and a cognitive test score improved more with vitamin D; sleep, depression, other cognitive tests and inflammation markers did not differ.

In a 36-week double-blind randomized trial in 65 people with ME/CFS, yeast beta-glucan combined with vitamin D3, vitamin B6 and zinc was compared with placebo. Cognitive fatigue improved compared with the supplement group's own starting point; the abstract does not report a difference from placebo.

In a 6-month randomized trial in 50 people with chronic fatigue syndrome, 100,000 units of vitamin D3 every 2 months was compared with placebo. Vitamin D levels rose, but fatigue scores and markers of blood-vessel health did not improve.

A 2017 meta-analysis of four randomized trials (570 people given vitamin D and 560 given placebo), all rated at low risk of bias, found a statistically significant but small-to-moderate effect on knee pain and concluded that vitamin D may not have a clinically significant effect on pain or on structural progression. A 2021 meta-analysis of six reports covering 1,599 people with knee osteoarthritis found better WOMAC pain and function scores with vitamin D but no significant change in cartilage volume or joint space width. The trials were in knee osteoarthritis.

Results are mixed. The abstract of a 2024 meta-analysis of 11 randomized trials with 3049 people is internally inconsistent: its conclusion states that vitamin D supplements did not significantly reduce CRP, ESR, the disease activity score (DAS28) or disability scores, and that responses varied widely between trials, yet the same abstract reports a pooled analysis in which pain scores and two versions of the disease activity score (DAS28-CRP and DAS28-ESR) were significantly lower. A 2020 meta-analysis of 6 trials with 438 people found small improvements in DAS28, ESR and tender joint count compared with placebo, but not in other outcomes. These abstracts do not say whether participants stayed on disease-modifying drugs.

Treatment: in a trial of 561 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease followed for about 2.3 years, 2,000 IU a day of alpha-tocopherol slowed decline in daily activities compared with placebo, a delay of about 6 months over the follow-up. A Cochrane review found no evidence that vitamin E improves cognition in Alzheimer's disease or mild cognitive impairment, or that it prevents progression from mild cognitive impairment to dementia. Prevention: a Cochrane review of vitamin and mineral trials in cognitively healthy people found low-certainty evidence of no effect of vitamin E on dementia incidence.

In a six-month double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial in 77 people with knee osteoarthritis, vitamin E (500 IU a day) showed no benefit over placebo for pain, stiffness or function at one, three or six months. In a 2-year double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 136 people with knee osteoarthritis, vitamin E (500 IU) did not change the loss of tibial cartilage volume, and symptom improvement did not differ from placebo. A 2022 meta-analysis of nutritional supplements reported that vitamin E caused no changes in osteoarthritis measures.

In a 12-week randomized double-blind trial, 42 people already taking anti-rheumatic drugs added vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol 600 mg twice a day) or placebo. Pain measures fell with vitamin E compared with placebo, but clinical signs of inflammation and laboratory inflammatory markers did not change. A 2023 meta-analysis of 9 publications, whose control groups received placebo, other drugs or external therapy, reported pooled differences in tender and swollen joints whose confidence intervals included no difference.

In an 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 64 women took vitamin K1 10 mg a day or placebo. A blood marker of joint destruction did not change, and rheumatoid factor did not differ between groups after adjustment. The abstract does not report joint counts or pain results, and does not say whether participants stayed on disease-modifying drugs.

A 2014 meta-analysis of randomized trials found no effect of bran on IBS symptoms, and a 2015 meta-analysis found insoluble fibre did not improve any outcome. In a 12-week placebo-controlled trial of 275 people in primary care, bran did better than placebo in the third month only, and that result was not statistically significant in the worst-case analysis; symptom severity after three months did not differ from placebo.

A systematic review of randomized trials of systemic treatments for alopecia areata concluded that the evidence does not support oral zinc sulphate; it does not report trials showing no benefit over placebo, so this is graded Insufficient rather than Negative. A 1981 double-blind trial of oral zinc sulphate exists, but no abstract is available to report its results. In an uncontrolled 12-week study of 15 people with low blood zinc, 50 mg of zinc gluconate a day raised zinc levels; 9 of the 15 had some regrowth, which the authors reported was not statistically significant. A meta-analysis of 34 papers on blood trace elements found lower blood zinc in people with alopecia areata than in healthy controls; that is an association, not evidence that supplements help.

A 2021 meta-analysis pooled 5 randomized trials of zinc added to antidepressant drugs in people with clinical depression and found a modest reduction in depressive symptoms compared with placebo, though the effect was not significant when trials were grouped by sample size. A 2022 meta-analysis of randomized trials found lower depression scores with zinc in depressed patients, but only when zinc was given on its own, and called for further trials of zinc alone versus added to other treatment. A 2016 review of nutrients added to antidepressants described the results for zinc as mixed.

In a 16-week double-blind randomized trial in 50 people with ME/CFS, melatonin (1 mg) with zinc (10 mg) once daily was compared with placebo. Physical fatigue was lower than with placebo at the final treatment visit, and the physical health summary score improved at every visit in the supplement group.

In a 36-week double-blind randomized trial in 65 people with ME/CFS, yeast beta-glucan combined with vitamin D3, vitamin B6 and zinc was compared with placebo. Cognitive fatigue improved compared with the supplement group's own starting point; the abstract does not report a difference from placebo.

grade_key.A: Meta-analysis, or at least 2 randomized trials with low risk of bias and a consistent benefit
grade_key.B: 1 good randomized trial, or several randomized trials with mixed results
grade_key.C: Observational studies, small pilots or open-label trials only
grade_key.Negative: Randomized trials found no benefit over placebo
